description: Reviewed FoodEx2 ontology-exception cases. These examples test transfer and negative controls outside runtime prompts; they are not prompt demonstrations.

cases.question: For dried non-tea herbal infusion material made from leaves, should I use raw A03JK without an explicit drying facet, or derivative A04KK?
cases.reference_answer: Use the appropriate raw herbal-infusion-material base, such as A03JK when its scope fits, without adding drying merely to restate the normally marketed dried state. Herbal infusion materials retain the marketed-dry raw exception. A04KK is a derivative scoped to dried or fermented Camellia sinensis tea leaves and does not cover non-tea herbal infusion materials.

cases.question: Does ordinary drying turn a marketed dried spice into a FoodEx2 derivative?
cases.reference_answer: No. Spices are a marketed-dry exception and remain raw commodities irrespective of drying. Do not add an explicit drying facet merely to restate their default dried state. If the spice is fresh, the non-default unprocessed status may be reported when relevant.

cases.question: Should dried or fermented Camellia sinensis tea leaves use the same raw-by-default treatment as herbal infusion materials?
cases.reference_answer: No. The 2015 split removed Camellia sinensis from the marketed-dry exception. Fresh Camellia sinensis leaves are raw; dried or fermented tea leaves follow the derivative path, for which A04KK is the relevant scoped group when the candidate coverage fits.

cases.question: Is a prepared herbal infusion beverage coded as the same raw material as the dried leaves used to brew it?
cases.reference_answer: No. First distinguish the dry herbal infusion material from the prepared beverage. The marketed-dry exception governs the dry material; a brewed herbal infusion is a beverage product and should use the appropriate beverage base rather than the raw dry-material base.
